KEY MESSAGE 1...

In the mid/upper-levels, a progressive troughing pattern was present 
across North America, with a vertically-stacked low embedded within 
a large-scale trough that was rotating over northern Manitoba. This 
feature trailed a downstream shortwave trough that was ejecting into 
the Canadian Maritimes, which has positioned the CWA within the 
inflection point of a convectively-contaminated, low-amplitude, 
shortwave ridge. The net increase in subsidence aloft, albeit 
slight, will result in the demise of a weak MCC advecting eastward 
across KY towards far southeastern OH and southwestern WV. Farther 
southwest, a broader mid-level trough, which is accompanied by a 
well-defined vorticity lobe, was pivoting eastward across the Ozark 
Mountains. The 12Z objectively analyzed UA charts also observed a 
sharply cyclonic 250 mb trough over AR as well, and is evident on 
water-vapor imagery. As this shorter-wave trough continues to eject 
northeastward towards the CWA over the next 24 hours, it will lose 
amplitude as it becomes absorbed into the base of the large-scale 
trough pivoting towards the Great Lakes region, with an expectation 
for the vorticity lobe to begin decaying as it rotates over the CWA 
amidst increasing divergence within the mid/upper-levels.

At the surface, a quasi-stationary front was draped across the Ohio 
River Valley and eastward into northern WV, with the northern edge 
of the stratus cloud deck demarcating its location. The front will 
remain stalled in an east-west-oriented manner for the rest of the 
day before undergoing warm-frontogenesis tonight as the shortwave 
trough over the Ozark Mountains ejects towards the CWA. Dewpoints 
were in the lower 70s across the moist sector/south of the front, 
while the northern zones have mixed into the middle 60s where full 
insolation is ongoing. The rain shield associated with the weak MCC 
will continue to progress eastward across the southern half of the 
CWA for the next few hours, but the weak UVVs should eventually 
succumb to the substantially overturned airmass and subsidence aloft 
from the presence of the low-amplitude ridge. Little change to the 
airmass is expected throughout the next 24 hours, with the exception 
of the northern counties that have mixed out on the northern side of 
the quasi-stationary front, as rapid boundary-layer moistening will 
occur following the passage of the warm front Saturday afternoon.

By Saturday morning, the compact vorticity lobe will have opened and 
become increasingly stretched as absorption into the large-scale 
troughing to the north commences. Isolated showers and thunderstorms 
will be possible across southeastern OH, northeastern KY, and far 
western WV by late Saturday morning, but the overnight and morning 
hours into Saturday will be otherwise benign, with the exception of 
valley fog. Greater coverage of heavy showers and storms will not 
arrive until the afternoon as the wave of more-vigorous ascent 
translates eastward over the CWA. The 12Z RAOB from BNA also sampled 
a tall, skinny EML; and was characterized by 1,347 J/kg and 1,802 
J/kg for mixed-layer and most-unstable parcels, respectively. This 
observation was also downstream of the shortwave trough and within 
the belt of broad, southwesterly flow aloft. Advection of this EML 
will accompany the ejection of the shortwave trough, with forecast 
soundings indicating CAPE values locally >2,000 J/kg in conjunction 
with cloud-layer shear of about 30 kt Saturday afternoon. 

Multiple clusters of heavy showers and storms are forecast to move 
from southwest-to-northeast across the CWA Saturday, with organized 
cores capable of producing efficient rainfall given warm-cloud 
depths ascending to as high as 15 kft AGL. Instantaneous rainfall 
rates may exceed 2"/hr. Moist-adiabatic lapse rates will also 
curtail the potential for strong winds, but a rogue, severe-caliber 
downburst or two cannot be entirely ruled out. Otherwise, the 
primary hazard associated with storms Saturday will be top-heavy 
towards the flash flooding risk. Locations that have experienced 
heavy rainfall, and in some cases, extreme rainfall, over the last 
36 hours will be especially susceptible to rapid rises of creeks and 
streams. A Flood Watch is now in effect for locations along and west 
of the I-79 and US-119 corridors between 12 PM EDT Saturday to 1 AM 
EDT Sunday.

KEY MESSAGE 2...

The base of the large-scale trough will dig southward across the 
Great Lakes region and into the Rust Belt during the afternoon hours 
Sunday. At the surface, the respective synoptic cold front will be 
approaching southeastern OH from the northwest, with the cold front 
continuing to move southeastward into WV by the latter half of the 
afternoon. A pre-frontal surface trough may serve as the impetus for 
isolated-to-widely-scattered showers and storms, with more-scattered 
coverage arriving as the cold front crosses through the CWA heading 
into Sunday
